area: Area X. Slow Flight, Stalls, and Spins
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why a pilot stalls a second time during a stall recovery, demonstrate a secondary stall safely from the right seat while you explain it, recover from it, and teach a learner how it links to low-altitude stalls, the go-around and the spin recovery.
why: Stall accidents usually come from an inadvertent stall at low altitude where the recovery is not finished before the ground [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], and near the ground a pilot's natural impulse is to bring the nose up as soon as possible and abruptly [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The secondary stall is what that impulse produces. The CFI ACS says the flight instructor normally demonstrates this stall to learners for familiarization and stall/spin awareness, so you need to show it safely and make the learner understand what they saw.

warmup: Think first: your learner stalls on a go-around with full flaps, 400 feet above the trees. They push, the horn stops, the nose is low and the trees fill the windshield. Their hands want to pull the yoke into their lap. What will the wing do if they pull now, why does the airspeed indicator not warn them, and what would you rather their hands did for the next three seconds?

key_terms.def: A stall that happens after the recovery from a stall that came before it [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
The AOA where the stall occurs; a given airplane always stalls at the same AOA regardless of airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
Its direction is set by the airplane's flight path in relation to the oncoming air, so a pull that changes attitude before the path changes raises the AOA [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
The ratio of the lift the wings produce to the weight of the airplane; stall speed rises with its square root [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].
Any stall above +1 G; most often inadvertent in badly flown turns, stall and spin recoveries and dive pull-outs [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
The critical AOA is exceeded; usually an uncommanded nose-down pitch that cannot be readily arrested, maybe with an uncommanded roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
The AOA causes a stall warning but has not reached the critical AOA [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
From the time the airplane stalls and rotation starts until the spin is fully developed [[13:12|AC 61-67C 110a]].
A nose-low, descending turn in which airspeed and G load can increase rapidly; the airplane is not stalled [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
The maximum speed with the flaps extended, the top of the white arc [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].
An uncontrollable, automatic muscle reflex set off by a sudden, intense event that violates the pilot's expectations [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Discontinuing a landing; its three cardinal principles are power, attitude and configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: Why you demonstrate the secondary stall

body.p: A secondary stall is named for when it happens: after the recovery from a stall that came first [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. A normal recovery points the nose toward the ground. If the stall happened at low altitude, the pilot's natural impulse is to bring the nose back up as soon as possible and to do it abruptly, and the closer the ground, the stronger the impulse [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The demonstration shows a learner, at a safe altitude, what that impulse does to the wing.

This lesson is narrow on purpose. AOA, stall cues, the recovery template and the learner who freezes are taught in Power-Off Stalls (AI.X.C) and Power-On Stalls (AI.X.D). Here we cover only what is specific to the second stall: what causes it, how to show it safely, how to recover, and how it ties to the go-around and to spins.

callout.text: CFI ACS Appendix 3, Area X: "The flight instructor normally demonstrates stall Tasks F, G, and H to learners for the purposes of familiarization and stall/spin awareness. Private and commercial pilot certification does not include these Tasks." For this Task: "Secondary stalls include a full stall." The AFH agrees: for pilot certification it is a demonstration-only maneuver that only flight instructor applicants may be required to perform on a practical test [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

body.p: The causes the sources give, which become your teaching points for S5:

bullets: Not enough nose-down: the pilot does not reduce the AOA enough by lowering the pitch attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
Power only: the pilot tries to break the stall with power alone [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Power reduces the altitude loss but does not eliminate a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
Hurry: the pilot tries to hasten the completion of the recovery before the airplane has regained sufficient flying speed [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

callout.text: Application: open the ground lesson with a picture, not a procedure. 'You just recovered from a stall 300 feet over the trees and the trees fill the windshield. What do your hands want to do?' Nearly every learner says 'pull'. That answer is the reason for the demonstration.

check.q: What three ways into a secondary stall do the AFH and AC 61-67C name?
check.a: Not reducing the AOA enough by lowering the pitch, trying to break the stall with power only [[24:123|AFH 5-18]], and hastening the recovery before sufficient flying speed returns [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

chunks.title: Aerodynamics: the nose moves before the flight path does

body.p: Aerodynamics of secondary stalls (K1). Start where every stall lesson starts: the critical AOA can be exceeded at any airspeed, attitude and power setting [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Then tell the secondary stall as a story about the relative wind:

bullets: The relative wind follows the flight path. The direction of the relative wind is set by the flight path in relation to the oncoming air [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. Application: right after the first recovery the path still points down, so the air meets the wing from below the direction the nose is about to point.

A sharp pull outruns the path. When a pilot in a dive pulls back sharply, gravity and centrifugal force prevent an immediate change of flight path, the AOA changes abruptly from quite low to very high, and the stall comes at a speed much greater than the normal stall speed [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

Load factor raises the stall speed. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]; an airplane with a 50-knot unaccelerated stall speed can be stalled at 100 knots at 4 G [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Abrupt pull-ups may produce recurrent or secondary stalls by increasing the AOA to the stalling angle [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].
The speed is not back yet. The AC names the cause plainly: completing the recovery before the airplane has regained sufficient flying speed [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

body.p: So the second stall is usually an accelerated stall. The AFH lists stall and spin recoveries among the places accelerated stalls most often happen inadvertently [[24:124|AFH 5-19]], and accelerated stalls are usually more severe than unaccelerated stalls and often unexpected because they come at higher-than-normal airspeeds [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104c]].

The trade-off. Recoveries from stalls and spins trade altitude loss (and more airspeed) against more load factor in the pull-up [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. A recovery that dives only to cruising or design maneuvering speed, with a gradual pull-up as soon as the airspeed is safely above stalling, needs no more than 2 or 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. The secondary stall happens when the pilot refuses to give up either: no more altitude and no time for speed.

callout.text: The nose moves at once; the flight path follows later. Pull before the path catches up, and the AOA pays the difference.

check.q: Why can a pilot pull into a second stall while the airspeed indicator shows well above the published stall speed?
check.a: The flight path cannot change at once, so a sharp pull raises the AOA abruptly [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]], and the added load factor raises the stall speed with its square root [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

chunks.title: Where secondary stalls happen for real

body.p: Flight situations where secondary stalls may occur (K2). Every row is a recovery, or a pull-up, near something the pilot wants to get away from:

head: Situation
What sets up the second stall
Source
rows: Stall at low altitude
The impulse to raise the nose as soon as possible and abruptly, stronger near the ground
Return to the flightpath after any stall
The template's last step: be careful to avoid a secondary stall, while staying aware of the terrain
Go-around climb with full flaps
After a full-flap stall recovery, climbing with the flaps out at a higher than normal pitch gives a secondary stall; in some airplanes even a normal climb pitch will
Rapid flap retraction
Retracting the flaps rapidly while holding a higher than normal climb pitch: a secondary stall or settling with a loss of altitude may result
Flap errors under distraction
AC 61-67C's power-off stall plan shows how errors in flap retraction can cause a secondary stall
Spin recovery pull-out
Too much or abrupt aft elevator can give a secondary stall and possibly another spin
Spiral recovery
Abrupt or excessive elevator inputs can lead to a secondary stall
Ice on the wing
After an upset, do not approach the upset AOA (or airspeed) again in the recovery, or another upset may occur; that AOA may be well below the normal stall AOA
Gusty approach
A gust can raise the AOA abruptly, and the stall may come while the pilot is trying to control the flightpath

body.p: Stall recovery procedure as a risk (R1). In this Task the recovery itself is the hazard. Every row above is a recovery done in the wrong order or too fast: the pilot reduced the AOA and then put it straight back.

callout.text: Stall accidents usually result from an inadvertent stall at low altitude with the recovery not completed before ground contact [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. A secondary stall is how a recovery that started in time still fails to finish.

check.q: AC 61-67C describes a go-around exercise after a full-flap, power-off stall. What produces the secondary stall in it?
check.a: Recovering, then trying to climb with the flaps still extended while holding a higher than normal climb pitch; in some airplanes a normal climb pitch is enough [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]].

body.p: Recognition of a secondary stall (K3) uses the same cues as any stall, but the learner is not expecting them: in their mind the stall is already over. Teach what is different:

bullets: The warning returns. The recovery holds nose-down input until the stall warning is eliminated [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. A horn, buffet or stick shaker [[24:117|AFH 5-12]] that comes back as the nose rises is the first sign of the second stall.

It comes at a higher speed. With the pull adding load factor, the stall comes at a speed much greater than the normal stall speed [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. A learner who trusts the airspeed indicator will not believe it; over-reliance on the airspeed indicator while excluding other cues after recovery is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Seat pressure. In a pull the G load pushes the pilot's body down in the seat [[24:124|AFH 5-19]], and an experienced pilot can judge load factor from seat pressure [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

The break. A full stall shows as an uncommanded nose-down pitch that cannot be readily arrested, perhaps with an uncommanded roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Because it is usually accelerated, expect it to be sharper than the first [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104c]].
Yaw at the break. If incorrect rudder use created the yaw, the pilot may not know the critical AOA is exceeded until the airplane yaws out of control toward the lowering wing [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

callout.text: Application: give the learner a phrase for the moment the warning comes back: 'Still stalled, push again.' A learner with words ready reacts faster than one who has to think of them.

check.q: In the pull-up after a recovery the horn sounds again at 70 knots, well above the book stall speed of 48. The learner says 'the horn is wrong.' What do you teach?
check.a: The pull adds load factor and AOA, so the airplane stalls at a speed much greater than normal [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]; trusting the airspeed indicator over the other cues after a recovery is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

body.p: The go-around is where most learners will meet a secondary stall for real. The maneuver is not dangerous in itself; it becomes dangerous when delayed unduly or executed improperly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Teach the two together:

bullets: Attitude: an airplane cannot fly below stall speed or climb below minimum power required speed, so resist any impulse to pitch up for a climb if the airspeed is insufficient; in some cases lower the nose briefly to gain airspeed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Trim: low-airspeed trim plus sudden power raises the nose, and letting it rise too early can mean an unrecoverable stall at low altitude [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Flaps: retract them in small increments so the airplane accelerates as they come up; a sudden, complete retraction can cause a loss of lift and settling [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Ground effect: the 'cushion' is borrowed performance, and an attempt to climb prematurely may leave the airplane unable to climb or even hold altitude at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

body.p: AC 61-67C gives you the bridge. After a full-flap, gear-extended, power-off stall, recover and attempt to climb with the flaps extended: a higher than normal climb pitch gives a secondary stall. Then recover and retract the flaps rapidly while holding that pitch: a secondary stall or settling with altitude loss may result [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]]. Application: fly this after the AFH demonstration, so the learner sees the same second stall come out of a realistic go-around rather than an abrupt pull.

Task prioritization (R5): in a go-around, airplane control is the first consideration in the high-workload phase, and reaching for the flap handle under high control pressures calls for caution [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Improper pitch attitude and climbing out of ground effect prematurely are listed go-around errors [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

callout.text: Go-around: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The right attitude is the one the airspeed allows, not the one the trees ask for.

check.q: On a go-around close to the runway, why does the AFH warn against climbing out of ground effect too early?
check.a: The extra performance near the ground is borrowed and is repaid on climbing out, so a premature climb may leave the airplane unable to climb or even hold altitude at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

chunks.title: From a second stall to a spin

body.p: A secondary stall comes with the learner's hands busy and the airspeed changing fast, which is when yaw creeps in. A spin needs one wing past the critical AOA with sideslip or yaw at or beyond the stall [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. If a stall is not recovered properly, a secondary stall or a spin may result [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

bullets: Yaw sources: incorrect rudder, adverse yaw from aileron, engine and propeller effects, and wind shear [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Proactively cancel yaw with rudder so a stall does not progress into a spin [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

The spin recovery has its own secondary stall: after rotation stops and the rudder is neutral, excessive back elevator can cause a secondary stall and may result in another spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Excessive back-elevator pressure after rotation stops is a listed spin error [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

Spiral, not spin: if the airspeed is increasing, the airplane is no longer in a spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. In a spiral recovery, raise the nose to a climb only after the speed decreases to safe levels [[24:131|AFH 5-26]], and avoid abrupt or excessive elevator that could cause a secondary stall [[13:13|AC 61-67C 112]].
Load in the pull-out: a proper spin recovery usually loads about 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]; avoid exceeding the G and airspeed limits during the pull-out [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

callout.text: If the second stall breaks with a wing drop and rotation starts, you have a spin entry. Use the POH spin recovery, which takes precedence over the AFH [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. In airplanes placarded against spins there is no assurance that recovery from a fully developed spin is possible [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Spin training itself is AI.X.I.

check.q: After a spin recovery your learner neutralizes the rudder, then hauls the yoke back hard to stop the dive. What do the AFH and AC 61-67C say can happen?
check.a: Excessive or abrupt back elevator can cause a secondary stall and possibly another spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]].

chunks.title: Entry procedure and minimum entry altitude

body.p: Entry procedure (K4). The AFH gives it in one sentence: to show how this occurs at altitude, the pilot makes an abrupt recovery after one stall and exceeds the critical AOA a second time [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The ACS adds a specified configuration (S3) and Appendix 3 adds the full stall. A workable sequence:

head: Step
What you do
Source
rows: Brief
On the ground: configuration, the two stalls, the recovery, who is flying, and your floor
CFI ACS Appendix 3: the applicant and the evaluator "must review this area of operation during the preflight briefing"
Altitude
Enter high enough to finish no lower than 3,000 ft AGL with room for two recoveries and a spin margin (S2)
Clear
Clear the area at and below your altitude (S1)
First stall
Set the specified configuration and fly a normal stall to the full stall: the uncommanded nose-down pitch (S3)
The mistake
Lower the nose, then raise it abruptly before flying speed returns
Second stall
Call the returning warning and the break (S3)
AI.X.H.S3
Recover
Nose down until the warning stops, wings level, coordinate, power as needed, then a gradual pull-out

callout.text: ACS, exactly. S2: "Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 3,000 feet above ground level (AGL)." S3: "Enter a stall in a specified configuration and exceed the critical angle of attach a second time during the recovery." (The ACS prints 'attach'; it means attack.)

body.p: Minimum entry altitude. The AFH recommends stall practice that allows recovery no lower than 1,500 ft AGL [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]; this Task asks for twice that. Losing altitude in a stall recovery is to be expected [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], and here there are two. Add your airplane's measured loss for both, and a spin margin: the first turn of a spin loses about 1,000 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

Configuration. Application: the abrupt pull of the AFH method is an accelerated stall, and the AFH says never to practice accelerated stalls with the flaps extended because of the lower design G limits in that configuration [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Fly the abrupt-pull version clean. Show the flaps-down secondary stall with AC 61-67C's gentler go-around method, holding a too-high climb pitch rather than yanking [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]]. Agree the configuration with the evaluator before flight.

callout.text: Application: pull firmly enough to make the second stall happen, not as hard as you can. The point is to show the AOA outrunning the flight path. A violent pull only adds G and makes the learner flinch.

check.q: Terrain under the practice area tops out at 1,800 ft MSL. Before adding any recovery loss or spin margin, what is the lowest altitude at which this demonstration may be completed?
check.a: 4,800 ft MSL: 1,800 + 3,000, since S2 requires completion no lower than 3,000 ft AGL (AI.X.H.S2). Then add the loss for two recoveries and about 1,000 ft for a spin's first turn [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

body.p: Recovery procedure (K5). If a secondary stall occurs, do the stall recovery again: nose-down elevator as required to eliminate the stall warning, level the wings with ailerons, coordinate with rudder and adjust power as needed. When the airplane is no longer stalled, return to the desired flightpath [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. AC 61-67C says the same: forward pressure or relaxing the back pressure again, then, with sufficient airspeed, back to straight and level [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].
What makes the second recovery different:

bullets: Nose: it may already be low. The forward pressure needed differs between airplanes, and too much can hinder recovery with a negative load on the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. Excessive forward-elevator pressure giving low or negative G is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

Speed: two nose-down recoveries in a row build speed fast. The airspeed indicator and tachometer must never reach their high-speed red lines in a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]], and excessive airspeed buildup is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Pull-out: dive only to cruising or maneuvering speed and pull up gradually once the speed is safely above stalling; that needs no more than about 2 or 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].
Coordination: cancel yaw through the whole sequence [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]; poor rudder coordination through the stall and recovery is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Terrain: return to the flightpath with smooth, coordinated inputs, avoiding another secondary stall while staying aware of terrain [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: The risk in the recovery (R1) points two ways. Too little nose-down, power first or an early pull gives the second stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Too much push gives negative G, and too long a dive gives excess speed and a harder pull-out [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. Teach the middle: push until the warning stops, let the speed come, then pull gently.

callout.text: Push till it's quiet, wait for the speed, then ease it up.

check.q: After the second stall your learner pushes until the horn stops, then holds the nose low until the airspeed nears the red line before pulling. What is going wrong?
check.a: Excessive airspeed buildup, a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; the airspeed must never reach the red line in a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]], and the faster the dive, the higher the load factor in the pull-up [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

body.p: Effect of environmental elements on airplane performance (R2). The ACS line for this Task names cross-controlled stalls, but turbulence, microbursts and high density altitude matter just as much to a secondary stall:

bullets: Turbulence: a vertical gust or wind shear can raise the AOA abruptly and stall the airplane at a significantly higher airspeed than in stable air [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. Application: in a pull-out already near the critical AOA, a gust can supply the second stall for you.

Microbursts: downdrafts of up to 6,000 fpm, and on takeoff a headwind, then downdrafts, then a rapidly increasing tailwind that can put the airplane into the terrain [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Near-ground sink is exactly what triggers the urge to pull [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Some microbursts cannot be escaped with any known technique [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]: avoid them.

High density altitude: indicated stall speed hardly changes, but true airspeed is higher for the same indicated airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]], and climb performance drops [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Spin altitude losses are greater at higher density altitudes [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]. Application: each recovery costs more altitude and the climb back takes longer.

body.p: Aircraft limitations (R4):

head: Limitation
Why it matters in this demonstration
rows: G limits with flaps out
Lower design G limits with the flaps extended; never practice accelerated stalls with them out [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]
VFE
The top of the white arc, the maximum speed with flaps extended [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]; two nose-down recoveries with flaps out can reach it fast
VA and abrupt inputs
No full or abrupt control movements at or above VA; large alternating inputs can cause structural failure even below VA [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]]
Red lines
Airspeed indicator and tachometer never at their red lines in a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]
Spin approval
Find it in the type certificate data, the AFM/POH limitations or a placard; a placarded airplane gives no assurance of recovery from a developed spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Aft CG
Less elevator force reaches a high AOA, inadvertent stalls come easier, and high load factors are easier to pull in the recovery [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]]

callout.text: Application: on the ramp, find VFE, VA for today's weight and the spin placard with the learner. Those three items decide how hard, and in which configuration, you may demonstrate.

check.q: Why does an aft CG make a secondary stall more likely in the pull-out?
check.a: With an aft CG, less elevator force reaches a high AOA, and in the recovery it is easier to generate higher load factors [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]].

body.p: Collision hazards (R3). This demonstration descends twice, so the airspace below matters most. Clear at and below your altitude [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Clearing should precede stalls and spins, and the attitude of the aircraft creates additional blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. Teach an effective clearing procedure and insist on its use [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]; you and the learner share the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
Distractions, task prioritization, loss of situational awareness, or disorientation (R5):

bullets: Distractions: stalls from poor airspeed management are most likely when the pilot is distracted by other tasks, such as finding a checklist or attempting a restart after an engine failure [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]]. Application: in a real secondary stall the distraction is the ground rushing up.
Task prioritization: AOA first. Attempting recovery without recognizing the importance of pitch control and AOA, and recovering with power before reducing AOA, are listed errors [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

Loss of situational awareness: knowing the aircraft's position and flight path [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Losing it and failing to return to the desired flightpath is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. After two stalls, check the altitude against your floor first.

Disorientation: many upsets happen while attention is on a task away from the instruments and outside references, and disoriented pilots may not know it [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Two nose-down pitches in a row are disorienting; recover by the horizon and cross-check the attitude indicator.

Startle: an automatic reflex to a sudden, intense event that violates expectations [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. The second stall is meant to surprise the learner's beliefs, not their reflexes, so brief it first.

callout.text: Do not teach stalls below a cloud layer that leaves too little altitude to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. The 3,000 ft AGL floor plus two recoveries often puts this demonstration well above your other stall work.

check.q: Why does this demonstration call for extra care clearing below you, compared with a single stall?
check.a: It has two stalls and two recoveries, each losing altitude [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], so you descend further into the airspace below; clear at and below your altitude, and remember the attitude creates more blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

chunks.title: Fly it while you explain it

body.p: Demonstrate in the order you briefed, explaining power settings, attitudes and other pertinent factors as you fly [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Learners imitate the instructor, so fly it exactly the way you want it learned, including every safety step [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. A script for a clean-configuration demonstration:

bullets: 1. 'Clear left, clear right, clear below. We are at 6,000; terrain is 1,300; we finish above 4,300.' (S1, S2)
2. 'Clean, power to idle, holding altitude, nose coming up.' Fly the first stall to the full stall: 'Buffet, horn, and the nose drops by itself. That is a full stall.' (S3) [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
3. 'Now the mistake. Nose down, and I am pulling it right back up before the speed is back, the way a pilot does when the ground is close.' [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
4. 'Feel the seat? That is load factor. Horn is back. Buffet. Second stall, at a higher speed than the first.' (S3) [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]
5. 'Recovery again: push until it is quiet, wings level, ball centered, power. Now I wait for the speed, and ease it up.' (S4) [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]

6. 'Where does this happen for real? A stall near the ground, a go-around with full flaps, the pull-out after a spin. The fix is the same: let the speed come back before you ask the wing for more.' (S5) [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]

S5
"Describe and demonstrate conditions that lead to a secondary stall for future avoidance."

body.p: Note the wording. The skills line for this Task reads 'The applicant exhibits the skill to', not 'demonstrates and simultaneously explains', but S5 asks you to describe the conditions, so narrate the whole time.

callout.text: Application: practice until you can say step 4 while your hands do step 5. If talking ever delays your push, stop talking; the recovery matters more than the words.

check.q: Which ACS element makes this more than a stall you fly, and what does it ask of you?
check.a: S5: "Describe and demonstrate conditions that lead to a secondary stall for future avoidance" (AI.X.H.S5). You explain the low-altitude pull [[24:123|AFH 5-18]], the full-flap go-around [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]] and the spin pull-out [[24:130|AFH 5-25]], not just fly the maneuver.

body.p: When. A learner can stall an airplane on the first attempt, but stall recovery cannot really be learned without some experience in normal flight, and time and practice are needed to develop a perception of the stall [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]. Application: show the secondary stall only after the learner flies full power-off and power-on stalls with confident recoveries; it builds on both.

On the ground. When introducing stalls, review the aerodynamics, then carefully describe the physical sensations to expect and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. For this Task the sensations are two nose-down pitches, seat pressure in the pull, and a horn that comes back after it went quiet. Tell the learner that you will fly it.
A lesson flow (application):

bullets: 1. Ground: draw the relative wind before and after the pull, and give the three causes [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].
2. Air: your demonstration, with the learner following lightly on the controls if they are comfortable [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
3. Fly it again while the learner tells you each step; a misunderstanding can be corrected before the learner is absorbed in controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
4. The realistic version: AC 61-67C's full-flap stall with the go-around climb, and the flap retraction errors [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200e]] [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]].
5. Carry it forward: watch the pull-out on every later stall. Inadvertent secondary stall during recovery is one of the AFH's common stall errors [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], so it will turn up again.

body.p: Get it right the first time: by the principle of primacy, the learner should get it right first [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Application: the first secondary stall a learner sees should be clean, coordinated and well narrated. A sloppy, yawing demonstration teaches fear, not the lesson.

Threat narrows perception: a frightened learner limits attention to whatever frightens them [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]. A learner still tense from the first stall may not perceive the second one at all. Pause and talk between demonstrations; one slow, well-explained pair beats several in a row.

callout.text: Application: in the debrief, ask 'Where on our next flight could this happen?' and wait. The answers you want are 'a go-around' and 'after a stall near the ground'.

check.q: Why does the AIH's time-and-opportunity point argue for showing the secondary stall after the basic stalls?
check.a: Stall recovery cannot really be learned without some experience in normal flight, and time and practice are needed to develop a perception of the stall [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]; the second stall only makes sense once the first recovery is understood.

chunks.title: Teaching safely: when the learner's reflex joins in

body.p: In this Task the danger is less your demonstration than the learner's reflex. An anxious learner's reaction to stalls may become fight or flight [[25:42|AIH 2-9]], and anxious learners can be incredibly strong [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. A learner following along who pulls in your dive is giving you a real, unplanned secondary stall.

head: What the learner does
What you see
What you do
rows: Pulls during your recovery dive
Back pressure fighting your push, horn back early
Take the controls, calmly announcing 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], and recover again [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]
Pushes hard in fright
Loose items float, learner lifts off the seat
Excessive forward pressure gives low or negative G [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; relax to just what eliminates the warning [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Presses one rudder pedal
Ball out, nose yawing toward the low wing
Yaw at the stall leads to a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]; coordinate, and take over if needed
Freezes
No callouts, rigid on the controls
Take over; later, take the procedure apart and demonstrate each stage [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]

bullets: Brief it: the preflight briefing covers how you will exchange the flight controls (CFI ACS Appendix 2), and you tell the learner you are flying the demonstration.

Guard: with potentially hazardous maneuvers be alert and ready to take control at any time, especially on a first attempt [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Never let a learner exceed your limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Mitigate: operate at a safe altitude and guard the controls, then consciously accept the risk that remains [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]. Practicing full stalls can result in inadvertent spins [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
Know the airplane: review the POH before instructing in it [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

Safety of flight: the applicant and the instructor or evaluator must always recognize and avoid operations that could lead to an inadvertent stall or spin and inadvertent loss of control (CFI ACS Appendix 2).

callout.text: Application: set your own stop point before takeoff, such as an altitude or a bank angle at which you abandon the demonstration and simply recover. The ACS floor is the minimum, not the plan.

check.q: Halfway through your nose-down recovery the learner following along pulls back hard. What does the AIH say to do, and why not share the controls?
check.a: Take the controls and calmly announce 'I have the flight controls'; anxious learners can be very strong, and nothing is gained by fighting for control during a recovery [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

body.p: The AFH gives 18 common errors for intentional stalls [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] and has no separate list for the secondary stall. The ones below decide whether a second stall happens, plus related spin and go-around errors, and two errors an instructor applicant makes in the demonstration itself. On the checkride the evaluator may play a learner and make them (S6).

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Inadvertent secondary stall during recovery [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Horn or buffet returns as the nose comes up
Push again, then let flying speed return before raising the nose [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]
Not maintaining nose-down input until the warning is eliminated [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Back pressure returns while the horn still sounds
Hold forward pressure until the warning stops [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Recovering with power before reducing AOA [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Hand to the throttle first, nose still high
Power reduces altitude loss but does not end a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Recovery without recognizing the importance of pitch control and AOA [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
'We are fast enough now' at the second horn
Teach AOA, not speed: the critical AOA can be exceeded at any airspeed [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
Over-reliance on the airspeed indicator after recovery [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Eyes locked on the airspeed during the pull-out
Add the other cues: outside attitude, seat pressure [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]], the horn
Poor rudder coordination through the stall and recovery [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Ball out in the dive or the pull
Cancel yaw throughout [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Excessive forward-elevator pressure [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Loose items float, learner off the seat
Only enough to eliminate the warning [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]
Excessive airspeed buildup [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Long dive, speed racing toward the red line
Gradual pull-up once safely above stalling [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]
Excessive back elevator after spin rotation stops [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Hard pull right after the rotation stops
Gentle pull to level flight within G and airspeed limits [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Improper pitch attitude on a go-around [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Nose high, speed low, flaps down
Resist the pitch-up until the airspeed allows it [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Applicant: no full stall first (application)
Recovery at the first chirp of the first stall
CFI ACS Appendix 3: "Secondary stalls include a full stall."
Applicant: abrupt pull with flaps out (application)
A hard yank with the flaps extended
Abrupt version clean [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]; flaps version by a gentle, too-high climb pitch [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]]

body.p: Misconception or motor skill? When the learner thinks out loud, it is easy to tell whether an error comes from a misconception or a simple lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. 'I pulled because we were losing altitude' is a misconception for the ground. A pull that is merely too quick needs smoother practice.

callout.text: Safety permitting, it is often better to let a learner go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. In this Task the margin is two stalls deep, so decide your limit before you fly.

check.q: The 'learner' recovers from the second stall, then keeps checking the airspeed and says 'we're at 75, we can't stall' while pulling hard. Name the errors and the fix.
check.a: Over-reliance on the airspeed indicator and recovery without recognizing the importance of AOA [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; the critical AOA can be exceeded at any airspeed [[24:117|AFH 5-12]], so pull gradually once safely above stalling [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

scenario.title: A go-around that almost stalled twice, then the demonstration
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. This morning your 30-hour private pilot learner bounced a full-flap landing, added full power and pulled the nose up steeply to 'get away from the runway'. The horn blared, you took the controls and flew the go-around. This afternoon you plan a secondary stall demonstration in a fixed-gear, high-wing trainer placarded against intentional spins. It is hot, the practice area terrain tops out at 1,100 ft MSL, cumulus bases are near 6,500 ft MSL, and there is light chop below 5,000 ft MSL. You measured about 300 ft lost per stall recovery in this airplane last month.

questions.q: In the sources' terms, what went wrong on this morning's go-around?
questions.a: The learner pitched up for a climb with insufficient airspeed; the AFH says to resist that impulse and sometimes lower the nose briefly to gain airspeed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. With full flaps, a higher than normal climb pitch after a stall gives a secondary stall [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]], and trying to climb out of ground effect early is a listed go-around error [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

questions.q: What is your lowest entry altitude, and does the cloud base allow it?
questions.a: Completion floor: 1,100 + 3,000 = 4,100 ft MSL (AI.X.H.S2). Add two recoveries at about 300 ft each (4,700) and about 1,000 ft for a spin's first turn [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]: enter near 5,700 ft MSL. That is only about 800 ft below the 6,500 ft bases; if the bases drop, do not teach it under them [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

questions.q: How do the heat and the chop change the demonstration?
questions.a: Indicated stall speed hardly changes, but true airspeed is higher and spin losses are greater at high density altitude [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]] [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]], and climb performance drops [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. In the chop a gust can raise the AOA abruptly [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]], so the pull-out may stall earlier than you intend; enter above it.

questions.q: The learner asks to see it 'with full flaps, like this morning'. How do you set it up?
questions.a: The abrupt-pull version is an accelerated stall, and accelerated stalls must not be practiced with flaps extended because of the lower G limits [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Fly that version clean. Show the flaps-down version with AC 61-67C's go-around method: recover from a full-flap stall and hold a higher than normal climb pitch [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]], watching VFE [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

questions.q: During your recovery dive the learner, following along, pulls back hard. What do you do?
questions.a: Take the controls and calmly announce 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], recover from any second stall with nose-down until the warning stops, wings level, coordinated, power as needed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]], then debrief why they pulled.

questions.q: How do you close the lesson so it prevents this morning's mistake?
questions.a: Describe the conditions that lead to a secondary stall for future avoidance (AI.X.H.S5): the urge to pull near the ground [[24:123|AFH 5-18]], the full-flap go-around [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]] and the go-around rule to keep the attitude the airspeed allows [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Then plan go-arounds at altitude on the next lesson.

skills.do: "Clear the area." Clear at and below your altitude before the first stall, and say what you are looking for.
skills.practice: Fly clearing turns with spoken callouts on every stall you fly, the way you want learners to copy them [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

skills.do: "Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 3,000 feet above ground level (AGL)." Explain how you added two recoveries and a spin margin.
skills.practice: Measure your airplane's altitude loss for one stall recovery with another instructor, then work out the entry for the highest terrain in your practice area [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

skills.do: "Enter a stall in a specified configuration and exceed the critical angle of attach a second time during the recovery": a full first stall, then an abrupt pull before flying speed returns, narrated.
skills.practice: With another instructor, fly the pair clean several times, pulling firmly but not violently, until the second stall comes on demand [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

skills.do: "Recover promptly and appropriately after a secondary stall occurs": nose down until the warning stops, wings level, coordinated, power as needed, then a gradual pull-out without excess speed.
skills.practice: Practice the second recovery until you pull out without a third warning and without approaching the red line [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

skills.do: "Describe and demonstrate conditions that lead to a secondary stall for future avoidance": the low-altitude pull, the full-flap go-around and the spin pull-out.
skills.practice: Teach the three situations to a friend in under three minutes, then fly the AC 61-67C go-around exercise at altitude [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]].

skills.do: "Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task" when the evaluator, as a learner, pulls early, recovers with power or trusts the airspeed indicator.
skills.practice: Have a fellow applicant fly stalls with planted errors while you name each one and its fix [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

quiz.q: Why is the secondary stall given that name?
options: It happens after the recovery from a stall that came before it
It is the stall of the second wing after the first wing has dropped
It follows the failure of the airplane's secondary flight controls
It is the stall that comes when a backup stall warning has failed
quiz.why: It is so named because it occurs after recovery from a preceding stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

quiz.q: Which cause of a secondary stall does AC 61-67C give?
options: Holding too much right rudder through the break of a power-on stall
Recovering on a predetermined heading during a turning stall entry
Trying to hasten the recovery before sufficient flying speed returns
Using nose-down trim instead of elevator to lower the nose at the break
quiz.why: A secondary stall is caused by attempting to hasten the completion of a stall recovery before the aircraft has regained sufficient flying speed [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

quiz.q: When a pilot pulls back sharply in a dive, why does the AOA jump?
options: The elevator stalls first, and the wing follows it a moment later
Gravity and centrifugal force keep the flight path from changing at once
The propeller slipstream over the wing is cut off by the sharp pull
The airspeed drops at once, so the wing must fly at a much higher AOA to keep its lift
quiz.why: Gravity and centrifugal force prevent an immediate change of flight path, so the AOA changes abruptly from low to very high [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

quiz.q: Per AC 61-67C, what do recoveries from stalls and spins trade against each other?
options: Rudder authority against aileron authority as the speed builds
Engine power against propeller efficiency in the dive
Heading accuracy against bank accuracy during the roll-out
Altitude loss (and more airspeed) against load factor in the pull-up
quiz.why: Recoveries from stalls and spins involve a tradeoff between loss of altitude (and an increase in airspeed) and an increase in load factor in the pullup [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

quiz.q: In AC 61-67C's go-around exercise, what may happen if the flaps are retracted rapidly while a higher-than-normal climb pitch is held?
options: The airplane accelerates quickly, so the climb rate improves
Nothing, as long as full power is set before the flaps move
A secondary stall, or settling with a loss of altitude
A pitch-down that needs nose-up trim to stop it
quiz.why: Retracting the flaps rapidly while holding a higher-than-normal climb pitch: a secondary stall or settling with a loss of altitude may result [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]].

quiz.q: Under CFI ACS Appendix 3, how far does the secondary stall Task go?
options: Recovery at the first indication of the first stall, every time
It includes a full stall
The evaluator chooses either an impending or a full stall
Impending stalls only, to protect the airplane from G loads
quiz.why: CFI ACS Appendix 3: "Secondary stalls include a full stall", and Task H is an exception to the evaluator's choice "where a full stall occurs". The AFH describes the full stall as an uncommanded nose-down pitch [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

quiz.q: What is the lowest height above the ground at which the CFI ACS lets this Task be completed?
options: 1,500 ft AGL, the AFH stall practice figure
2,000 ft AGL, the AFH figure plus a margin
2,500 ft AGL, half a spin turn above the AFH
3,000 ft AGL
quiz.why: AI.X.H.S2: completed no lower than 3,000 ft AGL. The AFH's general stall recommendation is 1,500 ft AGL [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

quiz.q: In a go-around, what does the AFH say about pitching up when the airspeed is low?
options: Resist the impulse to pitch up for a climb; lower the nose briefly if needed
Pitch up at once to the Vx attitude so the airplane clears any obstacles that lie ahead of it
Hold the landing attitude until the flaps are fully retracted first
Pitch up as far as the stall horn allows, since that is the best climb
quiz.why: The pilot should resist any impulse to pitch up for a climb if airspeed is insufficient, and may lower the nose briefly to gain airspeed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: After spin rotation stops and the rudder is neutralized, what can excessive back elevator cause?
options: A spiral dive with rapidly increasing airspeed
Nothing, since the wing is no longer stalled
A secondary stall and possibly another spin
A flat spin that cannot be recovered
quiz.why: Excessive back elevator pressure can cause a secondary stall and may result in another spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

quiz.q: What does the last step of the AFH stall recovery template warn about?
options: Returning to the flightpath carefully to avoid a secondary stall, while watching terrain
Retracting the speedbrakes before power is added, so that lift and the stall margin both improve together
Disconnecting the autopilot last, after the wings are level and the power is set
Trimming fully nose-up so the airplane climbs back to altitude on its own
quiz.why: Step 6: return to the desired flightpath with smooth, coordinated inputs, careful to avoid a secondary stall, while aware of terrain [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

final_quiz.q: Your 'learner' recovers from a full stall by adding full power with the nose still slightly high. The horn keeps sounding, then the airplane breaks again. Which cause is this?
options: Lowering the nose too far, giving negative G on the wing
Trying to break the stall with power only
Recovering on a predetermined heading
Retracting the flaps too slowly after the break
final_quiz.why: A secondary stall may occur when the pilot does not reduce the AOA enough or attempts to break the stall by using power only [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]; power reduces altitude loss but does not eliminate a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

final_quiz.q: Terrain tops out at 2,200 ft MSL. You lose about 400 ft per stall recovery and want a margin for a spin's first turn. What is the lowest entry altitude for this demonstration?
options: 5,200 ft MSL
6,000 ft MSL
6,200 ft MSL
7,000 ft MSL
final_quiz.why: Floor 2,200 + 3,000 = 5,200 (AI.X.H.S2); two recoveries 2 x 400 = 800 gives 6,000; first spin turn about 1,000 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] gives 7,000 ft MSL.

final_quiz.q: The 1 G stall speed is 48 knots. In the pull-out your learner reaches 2 G at 65 knots. Will the wing stall?
options: Yes: at 2 G the stall speed is about 68 knots
No: 65 knots is well above the 48-knot stall speed
No: at 2 G the stall speed is about 58 knots
Yes: at 2 G the stall speed doubles to 96 knots
final_quiz.why: Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]: 48 x 1.414 = 67.9 knots, above the 65 knots flown, so the wing stalls.

final_quiz.q: The evaluator asks for the demonstration in the landing configuration with full flaps. What is the soundest plan?
options: Use full flaps and the AFH abrupt pull, since the ACS lets the evaluator specify it
Decline the Task, because the ACS allows only the clean configuration for it
Use full flaps but recover at the first indication, never at the full stall
Show it by holding a too-high climb pitch after recovery, not by an abrupt pull
final_quiz.why: Accelerated stalls must not be practiced with flaps extended because of the lower design G limits [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]; AC 61-67C produces the flaps-down secondary stall with a higher-than-normal climb pitch [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]]. The ACS requires a full stall (Appendix 3).

final_quiz.q: A learner asks how they can sense the load factor building in a pull-out without an accelerometer. What do the sources offer?
options: Control pressure, which is the same in every airplane
The airspeed indicator, which shows load factor directly
Seat pressure, which an experienced pilot can judge
The slip-skid ball, which moves aft under load
final_quiz.why: Control leverage varies between airplanes, so pressure is not an index, but load factor can be judged from seat pressure [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]; the G load pushes the pilot down in the seat [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: In a spiral dive recovery, your learner rolls level and immediately pulls hard toward the horizon at high speed. What do the sources say?
options: Raise the nose only after the speed decreases; abrupt elevator can cause a secondary stall
That is correct; the faster the nose comes up, the less altitude the spiral dive will cost the pilot overall
The pull is fine as long as power stays at full until the nose reaches the horizon
Rolling level first is the error; the pull should come before the roll every time
final_quiz.why: Raise the nose to a climb only after speed decreases to safe levels [[24:131|AFH 5-26]], and avoid abrupt or excessive elevator that could lead to a secondary stall [[13:13|AC 61-67C 112]].

final_quiz.q: Why is the pull-out after a stall recovery more exposed to a gust-induced stall than cruise flight?
options: Gusts are stronger at the low airspeeds used in a pull-out
The wing is already working near the critical AOA, and a gust raises it abruptly
The critical AOA drops during a hard pull, so even a small gust reaches it much more easily
The stall horn is disabled by the high load factor
final_quiz.why: A vertical gust can cause an abrupt increase in AOA and a stall at a significantly higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]; the critical AOA itself does not change [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: After your demonstration the learner says, 'So the lesson is never to pull up after a stall.' What is the best reply?
options: Right: stay in the dive until reaching cruise speed, then level off with trim
Pull up, but gradually, once the airspeed is safely above stalling
Right: lowering the nose further is always safer than any pull-up
Pull up at once, but with full power so the wing cannot stall again
final_quiz.why: Dive only to cruising or maneuvering speed and pull up gradually once safely above stalling; that needs no more than 2 or 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. Excess airspeed buildup is itself a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AFH's warning about spin placards matter more in this demonstration than in an impending stall lesson?
options: A placard means the stall warning is not certified to work
A placard sets a lower minimum altitude for full stalls
A full stall followed by a sharp second stall invites yaw, and a placarded airplane has no assured recovery from a developed spin
Placarded airplanes cannot be stalled with the power at idle
final_quiz.why: A spin needs a stall plus yaw [[24:127|AFH 5-22]], and in airplanes placarded against spins there is no assurance that recovery from a fully developed spin is possible [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: In the debrief your learner says, 'The second stall happened because we were too slow.' How do you correct this?
options: Agree: the airspeed was below the published stall speed both times, so it simply ran out of lift
Agree: low airspeed causes every stall, so speed is the thing to watch
Explain that the flaps caused it, since flaps raise the stall AOA
Explain that the AOA passed the critical AOA, at a higher speed than the first stall
final_quiz.why: A stall comes from exceeding the critical AOA at any airspeed [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]; the sharp pull raised the AOA and the stall came at a speed much greater than normal [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: Which AC 61-67C power-off stall exercise is meant to show how flap retraction errors can cause a secondary stall?
options: Repeating the full-flap stall while you distract the student during the stall and recovery
Flying slow flight with the airspeed indicator covered and various flap settings
Gliding turn stalls from coordinated, slipping and skidding turns
An elevator trim stall from a trimmed landing approach descent
final_quiz.why: Have the student repeat the full-flap stall, distract them during the stall and recovery, and show how errors in flap retraction can cause a secondary stall [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200e]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing in icing, your airplane buffets and pitches down at an airspeed well above normal. After you recover, what does AC 61-67C warn about?
options: Hold the same pitch as before the upset, since the ice has now been shed
Do not approach the upset AOA or airspeed again, or another upset may occur
Raise the nose quickly to climb out of the icing layer before more forms
Extend full flaps to lower the stall speed back to its normal value
final_quiz.why: Note the AOA (or airspeed) at the upset and do not approach it during the recovery or another upset may occur; it may be well below the normal stall AOA [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102b]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner lifts off in ground effect on a go-around after a bounce and immediately pitches up steeply. What does the AFH say may happen?
options: The airplane may not climb or even hold altitude at full power
Ground effect will hold the airplane up until it reaches Vy
The steep pitch is fine because ground effect lowers the stall AOA
Nothing, provided the flaps are fully retracted first
final_quiz.why: An attempt to climb prematurely may leave the airplane unable to climb or even maintain altitude at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]; the performance in ground effect is borrowed [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

takeaways: A secondary stall follows the recovery from a first stall, when the pilot pulls before flying speed returns, lowers the nose too little, or uses power only.
The nose moves at once but the flight path does not, so a sharp pull raises the AOA and the stall comes at a higher speed.
Recover the same way again: nose down until the warning stops, wings level, coordinated, power, then a gradual pull-out.
The CFI ACS asks for a full stall first and completion no lower than 3,000 ft AGL; plan for two recoveries and a spin margin.
Fly the abrupt-pull version clean; show the flaps-down version with a too-high climb pitch, as in AC 61-67C.
Tie it to the go-around (attitude the airspeed allows) and to the spin and spiral pull-outs (gentle back pressure).
Guard the controls: a learner who pulls during your recovery turns a demonstration into a real second stall.
cfi_notes: The ACS S3 reads 'exceed the critical angle of attach a second time'. 'Attach' is a misprint for attack; quote it as printed if asked, and say so.

R2 for this Task names 'cross-controlled stalls', apparently carried over from Task F. Teach the environmental effects as they apply to the secondary stall (gusts in the pull-out, microburst sink near the ground, density altitude) and mention cross-control only in passing.

Altitude: the AFH recommends stall practice that allows recovery no lower than 1,500 ft AGL [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], and AC 61-67C uses 1,500 ft AGL for single-engine stall training [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]]. The CFI ACS asks 3,000 ft AGL for this Task (AI.X.H.S2). Fly the ACS figure plus two recoveries and a spin margin.

The AFH gives no configuration for the demonstration and the ACS says only 'a specified configuration'. Because the AFH abrupt pull is an accelerated stall and accelerated stalls are not to be practiced with flaps extended [[24:124|AFH 5-19]], brief the configuration with the evaluator and keep the flaps-down version gentle.

Two methods exist and both are in the sources: the AFH abrupt recovery after one stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] and AC 61-67C's go-around climb at a higher-than-normal pitch with flaps out [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]]. Use the first to show the mechanism and the second to show the real situation.

Recovery order: AC 61-67C paragraph 105 puts maximum allowable power right after reducing AOA [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]; the AFH secondary stall recovery says adjust power as needed after the wings are level and coordinated [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. After two nose-down recoveries the speed may already be high, so teach the AFH 'as needed'.

No source says in one sentence that a secondary stall is an accelerated stall. The AFH lists stall and spin recoveries among the places accelerated stalls happen [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] and the PHAK says abrupt pull-ups can produce secondary stalls by raising the AOA [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]; present the link as reasoning from those lines.

The ACS skills line for this Task says 'The applicant exhibits the skill to', not 'demonstrates and simultaneously explains'. Narrate anyway: S5 asks you to describe the conditions, and learners imitate the instructor's demonstration [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

AC 90-109A notes an airplane should show no tendency for a control-induced secondary stall, and that owners should learn to optimize stall recovery without entering one [[57:9|AC 90-109A p. 9]]. When you instruct in an unfamiliar or experimental airplane, find out how it behaves before you demonstrate this to a learner.
gaps: None of the sources gives the altitude lost in a secondary stall demonstration in a light trainer. Measure your airplane's loss for one recovery at altitude with another instructor and double it.

The sources do not say how hard to pull or how far to lower the nose before the pull in the demonstration; the AFH says only 'abrupt'. Agree the technique with the evaluator and stay within the POH limits.
Flap-extended G limits, VFE, VA at today's weight and spin approval come from the POH/AFM and placards, not the handbooks.
No source says whether a learner should fly a secondary stall themselves or how many demonstrations to give; the AFH calls it demonstration-only for certification. Follow your syllabus.
No source gives a script or exact briefing words for this demonstration. Write your own and use it every time.

activities.title: True or false: the second stall
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A secondary stall can happen after any stall, not only after a power-off stall.
cards.why: True. The AFH says this stall may occur after any stall when the pilot does not reduce the AOA enough or uses power only [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

cards.s: Once the stall horn stops during a recovery, the wing cannot stall again until the airspeed drops below the published stall speed.
cards.why: False. A sharp pull can raise the AOA to the stalling angle at a speed much greater than the normal stall speed [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

cards.s: Accelerated stalls are usually more severe than unaccelerated stalls.
cards.why: True. They are usually more severe and often unexpected, because they come at higher-than-normal airspeeds [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104c]].

cards.s: The pilot's urge to pull the nose up abruptly after a stall gets weaker closer to the ground.
cards.why: False. The reaction is amplified as proximity to the ground increases [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

cards.s: Adding full power is enough to recover from a secondary stall if the nose stays where it is.
cards.why: False. Power reduces altitude loss but does not eliminate a stall; reducing the AOA is imperative [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

cards.s: The recovery from a secondary stall is the same as from the stall before it.
cards.why: True. Nose-down elevator to eliminate the warning, wings level, coordinate with rudder, adjust power [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

activities.title: Numbers for the brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your trainer's 1 G stall speed is 48 knots. The PHAK says a good pull-out needs no more than 2 to 2.5 G. At 2.5 G, at what speed will the wing stall?
items.why: Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]: square root of 2.5 = 1.581; 48 x 1.581 = 75.9, about 76 knots.

items.q: By what percent does the stall speed rise when the pull-out reaches 2 G?
items.why: Square root of 2 = 1.414, so the stall speed is 1.414 times the 1 G value: (1.414 - 1) x 100 = 41.4, about 41 percent [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

items.q: Practice area terrain tops out at 1,300 ft MSL. You lose about 350 ft per stall recovery, this demonstration has two, and you add 1,000 ft for a spin's first turn. What is the lowest entry altitude?
PHAK example: an older airplane that stalls at 60 knots is stalled at 102 knots, 1.7 times its stall speed. What load factor does it undergo?
items.why: Load factor equals the square of the speed ratio: 1.7 x 1.7 = 2.89 G [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. A pull at a higher speed costs G fast.

activities.title: CFI checkride: the evaluator plays your learner
activities.intro: You are the CFI applicant. The evaluator acts as a private pilot learner who has never seen a secondary stall. Terrain in the practice area tops out at 1,600 ft MSL, you lose about 300 ft per recovery, and the airplane is placarded against spins.

steps.s: On the ground the 'learner' asks you to show it 'with full flaps and a really hard pull, like a real go-around'. Your answer?
options: Agree; the evaluator may specify any configuration and a hard pull is most realistic
Fly the hard pull clean, and show the flaps-down version with a too-high climb pitch instead
Refuse the flaps entirely; a secondary stall cannot happen with flaps extended
Agree, but only to the first indication so the G stays low
steps.why: Accelerated stalls are not practiced with flaps extended because of the lower G limits [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]; AC 61-67C shows the flaps-down secondary stall with a higher-than-normal climb pitch [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]].

steps.s: Level at 5,600 ft MSL, the 'learner' says 'this is plenty high, let's go.' What do you say?
options: Agreed, 5,600 is 4,000 ft above the terrain
Agreed, the AFH asks only 1,500 ft AGL
Not yet: climb to about 5,000 ft MSL or lower for realism
Not yet: we need about 5,200 to finish plus 1,000 for a spin, so about 6,200
steps.why: 1,600 + 3,000 = 4,600 (AI.X.H.S2); two recoveries at 300 ft = 5,200; about 1,000 ft for a first spin turn [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] gives about 6,200 ft MSL.

steps.s: After your first full stall you lower the nose. The 'learner', following on the controls, starts pulling back hard. What do you do?
options: Say 'I have the flight controls', take them and recover
Let them pull; it is the demonstration anyway
Push harder against them until they let go
Add full power so the pull cannot stall the wing
steps.why: Take the controls and calmly announce 'I have the flight controls'; nothing is gained by fighting an anxious learner for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

steps.s: Now the 'learner' flies the recovery after your second stall: horn stops, then they hold the nose low as the speed nears the yellow arc. What do you say?
options: Good, more speed means more margin; keep diving
Pull hard now to stop the dive before the red line
Start a gradual pull now; the speed is safely above stalling
Add full power to get the speed up faster
steps.why: Pull up gradually once the airspeed is safely above stalling, using no more than 2 to 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]; excessive airspeed buildup is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

steps.s: Back at altitude, the evaluator asks: 'Where will my learners meet this for real?' Your best answer?
options: Mostly in steep turns at cruise speed
Only in aerobatic airplanes during loops
After a stall near the ground, on a full-flap go-around, and in spin or spiral pull-outs
Only when the stall warning system has failed
steps.why: The urge to pull grows near the ground [[24:123|AFH 5-18]], the full-flap go-around climb [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]], and spin and spiral pull-outs [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[13:13|AC 61-67C 112]] (AI.X.H.S5).
